report.source_text: Native T1-mapping demonstrated markedly elevated T1 values with preponderance in the inferoseptal wall (1068 ± 73 ms in the entire slice vs. 1122 ± 31 ms in the inferoseptal wall), also see Figs. 1a and 2a. Furthermore, T2-mapping revealed increased values (entire slice 52 ± 6 ms, inferoseptal wall 55 ± 6 ms), suggesting myocardial edema representing active myocardial inflammation by hantavirus infection. In contrast, the LGE image, potentially indicating irreversible myocardial damage if positive, in the corresponding slice was negative (Fig. 1c).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 36-year-old male presented to the emergency department with headache and abdominal pain, accompanied by acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.0-3.0 mg/dl), massive proteinuria, thrombocytopenia (71,000/μl), and ECG abnormalities (sinus bradycardia 40/min, T-wave inversion in V2, incomplete RBBB). Puumala virus infection was confirmed by positive IgG/IgM ELISA and immunoassay. Six days after admission, the patient developed cardiac symptoms (chest pain and dyspnea). Workup revealed elevated cardiac biomarkers (high-sensitivity troponin I 0.32 μg/l [normal <0.04], creatine kinase 319 U/l [normal max 190]) without dynamic ECG changes. Cardiac MRI demonstrated myocardial inflammation characterized by elevated native T1-mapping (1068±73 ms entire slice, 1122±31 ms inferoseptal) and T2-mapping values (52±6 ms entire slice, 55±6 ms inferoseptal) indicating myocardial edema, despite negative late gadolinium enhancement. Coronary artery disease was excluded by coronary CT angiography performed after creatinine normalization. The patient received supportive therapy and showed rapid clinical improvement over the following weeks with resolution of chest pain and dyspnea.
